The United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s second visit to India this year has yielded little in terms of results

The United States Secretary of State’s three-day visit to India, his second in five months, came at a significant time in U.S. politics. Marco Rubio’s Mumbai trip this week was just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, which would mark the midpoint of President Donald Trump’s second term in office — a point at which the incumbent normally begins to focus on legacy, and possible contenders for the next Presidential election (Mr. Rubio is expected to be one), and start to look for possible partners and friendships around the world. In addition, his visit also raised hopes in New Delhi of a reset in bilateral ties, battered by two years of uncertainty over the Trump administration’s actions. This would include positive moves towards concluding the Bilateral Trade Agreement, reassuring India about U.S. sanctions on the import of Russian oil, preparations for upcoming Trump meets with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Manila (ASEAN) and Miami (G-20) summits, discussing plans for the Quad Summit (on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit) that India has been trying to host, and setting a date for Mr. Trump’s India visit. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s invitation also offered Mr. Rubio an opportunity to meet their UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to discuss the Gulf situation and to restore energy security and connectivity. And finally, Mr. Rubio’s visit to the Jamnagar Reliance refinery, led to speculation of some major deals on energy, possibly offering more discounts as he pitched for India to buy more American and U.S.-licensed Venezuelan oil.

Given all the high expectations, the visit was bound to come up short. The optics of his visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar, but not New Delhi, which was announced by the U.S. Ambassador to India, gave the Opposition fodder to question the real purpose of the visit. Despite Mr. Rubio’s two visits to India and more than six by Mr. Jaishankar to the U.S. since Mr. Trump took office, relations remain on edge, with issues on trade, tariffs, H-1B restrictions and anti-immigrant measures unaddressed. Also, the U.S.’s narrative on Operation Sindoor (2025), growing ties with Pakistan, and the Trump administration’s rhetoric on India’s economy, diaspora and Russian oil trade have added to India’s unhappiness. The two sides did not announce any agreements and Mr. Jaishankar and Mr. Rubio did not hold a joint press address. However, as they did at the U.S. Independence Day’s 250th anniversary celebrations in Delhi in May, they attended the “Freedom 250” event in Mumbai. Mr. Rubio acknowledged that while no two countries would agree on all issues, he said the U.S.-India alignment on core issues of national interest was “extraordinary”. item.title: Canary in the coal mine: On the performance of India’s core industrial sectors
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: Core sector gains may prove short-lived as September’s growth surge may not last
item.content:encoded:
Core sector gains may prove short-lived as September’s growth surge may not last

The latest data on the performance of the core industrial sectors show the economy may be facing an industrial uptick, but questions about its sustainability remain. Growth in the Index of Core Industries rose to a series-high of 7.9% in September 2026, the second consecutive month of accelerated performance. Any such improvement is to be celebrated, but a deeper look at what is driving it is also warranted. The coal sector saw growth suddenly shoot up to 10.7% in September. The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. The electricity sector grew 11.4% in September, capping off a half-year dominated by double-digit growth. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. The uptick in steel did, however, result in a return to double-digit growth for the iron ore sector, which should bode well for the mining component of the larger Index of Industrial Production.

The performance of the crude oil, natural gas, and refinery products sectors also highlights the fiscal problems India faces. At a time when the crude oil and natural gas sectors have both contracted continuously since 2024, refinery output rose to 10.3% in September. This means that the refineries were increasingly processing expensive imported oil. India’s oil imports in September were up 7% by volume but jumped 47% in terms of value due to the high price of oil. This is set to worsen. The attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have already pushed global oil prices above $112 a barrel, almost a six-month high. The reprieve from the U.S. on potential tariffs linked to imports of Russian oil provide India a reliable source, but the days of discounts are long gone. It is the time of premium pricing, and each barrel imported is eating into India’s foreign exchange reserves, which are also being used to defend the rupee. Cement and steel are the only sustainably growing core sectors, and those too are based on government infrastructure spending. At a time when industrial output is only temporarily propped up, the government’s fiscal space is fast shrinking.

item.title: Tunnelling through: On China’s export control list, tunnel-boring machines
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: China's export control list decision must push India to pursue domestic manufacturing alongside international partnerships and develop shared industrial capabilities
item.content:encoded:
China's export control list decision must push India to pursue domestic manufacturing alongside international partnerships and develop shared industrial capabilities

The Chinese Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs decision to place tunnel-boring machines (TBMs) on an export control list reveals a blind spot in India’s supply chain diversification. The curbs include TBMs, walking excavators, and high-altitude wet shotcrete machines. From November 18, if a shipment is intended for countries or regions deemed sensitive due to ongoing disputes with China, exporters will need an export licence from commerce authorities. For other countries/regions, exporters will need to be registered, obtain an export certificate, and submit end-use declarations stating that the equipment will not be re-routed to sensitive locations. While China has cornered around 70% of the global TBM market, prominent manufacturers in the West also maintain substantial component supply chains in the country to cut manufacturing overhead. Further, TBMs are complex to build as they have to be configured to geological characteristics at the project site and perform numerous tasks. Where a suitable TBM exists, it can be used for civilian or military purposes. India has struggled with TBM-related hold-ups with China for at least two years now, including for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project. Germany’s Herrenknecht AG set up an assembling and refurbishing facility in Chennai in 2007-08. TBM production economics differ significantly from conventional construction equipment as new plants need a minimum number of orders and must be able to access the industrial capability required to design, manufacture and repair specialised components.

However, even though India is one of the world’s largest TBM importers, expecting every sophisticated machine to be produced domestically will send public infrastructure costs soaring. Even now, depending on China’s decision on the TBMs set for India, India may have to redirect its procurement to facilities based directly in Germany or Japan, say, and absorb the higher capital cost. The BEML experience shows that manufacturing partnerships can fail without secure licensing arrangements and access to sustained demand. India should pursue domestic manufacturing alongside international partnerships, e.g., making equipment in the country under agreement with established foreign firms, and develop shared industrial capabilities rather than singular ‘national champions’, as TBM manufacturers and their suppliers can benefit from access to common testing and precision manufacturing infrastructure. Overall, Beijing is systematically identifying sectors where it commands a significant global capacity and establishing export controls to counter western technological restrictions, such as on advanced semiconductors, so any critical infrastructure sector relying on Chinese supply lines will face a compounding geopolitical risk.

item.title: Peace for progress: on the SCO, regional cooperation, the fight against terror

The SCO's effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s address at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, on Tuesday marks another significant occasion since Operation Sindoor (2025) when India has used the multilateral forum to raise the issue of terrorism, including cross-border terrorism from Pakistan. He said that regional cooperation cannot be meaningful if countries approached terrorism selectively. Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar’s presence added significance to the remarks, underscoring New Delhi’s diplomatic challenge within an organisation whose members have divergent strategic interests and security priorities. India has consistently argued that terrorism cannot be divorced from the broader agenda of regional peace, economic integration and development. By calling on SCO member-states to dismantle the ecosystem of terrorism, he reiterated that the threat must be addressed at its source rather than treated as an isolated security challenge. The intervention follows India’s refusal to endorse the joint statement at the 2025 SCO Defence Ministers’ meet in Qingdao, China. New Delhi had objected to a draft that failed to reflect its concerns over cross-border and Pakistan-sponsored terrorism, including the Pahalgam attack (2025), while referring to militant activities in Balochistan. India maintained that such an approach would undermine the organisation’s credibility by overlooking the threat it had brought before its members.

The SCO has the potential to advance regional stability, trade and connectivity instead of becoming another source of strategic friction. Yet, its effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats. India’s position is not that cooperation on trade, culture, connectivity and development must be suspended until every security dispute is resolved. Rather, these objectives cannot be met independently of a stable security environment. Economic corridors require predictable borders, investors need confidence in the rule of law, and transport networks must be violence- and disruption-free. Connectivity projects such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the development of Chabahar Port offer Central Asia connectivity with wider markets. Their long-term value, however, depends on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, alongside conditions that allow goods, capital and people to move freely. The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

item.title: Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India must extend restrictions to all forms of added sugars in foods meant for infants
item.content:encoded:
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India must extend restrictions to all forms of added sugars in foods meant for infants

The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

item.title: Fall of the centre: on the public discontent in France

item.description: To understand the precarious situation France is in today, all one has to do is to look at the macroeconomic numbers
item.content:encoded:
To understand the precarious situation France is in today, all one has to do is to look at the macroeconomic numbers

When Emmanuel Macroncame to power in 2017, at age 39, he promised to keep extremist political forces at bay, build a new France through his ‘revolution’, rejuvenate economic growth, manage debt and create employment opportunities. Nine years later, with six months to go for France’s next presidential election, Mr. Macron, whose approval rating is at an abysmally low 15%, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who lacks a parliamentary majority, are struggling to restore order in a country battered by economic woes, street protests, violent riots and a surging far right. Even in France, where protests are part of the political culture, Saturday’s (October 17, 2026) riots and looting were a shock with at least 3,000 businesses and shops damaged. Municipal halls were attacked and buildings set on fire, including the 19th-century Limoges town hall. Some 2,400 people were arrested and Prime Minister Lecornu called for local curfews. The trigger for the unrest was a move by Mr. Lecornu to pass budget proposals raising some taxes and freezing spending on social programmes. When school students hit the streets with demands for better educational facilities, the government responded with force and tear gas. But its heavy-handed response helped the student protest snowball into an anti-government movement, culminating in riots.

To understand the precarious situation France is in today, all one has to do is to look at the macroeconomic numbers. Growth remains sluggish with the economy estimated to expand by a mere 0.8% in 2026, while the unemployment rate stands at 8.3%. The core problem is the country’s public finances. France’s national debt stands at 120% of GDP, the third highest in the eurozone, after Greece and Italy. The French Treasury’s debt servicing bill is expected to reach about €60 billion in 2026. When Mr. Macron came to power, he reduced corporate taxes and sought to restrain public spending to stimulate growth. But growth remained sluggish while public debt ballooned. When protests gripped the country in 2018-19, he offered economic concessions, but with no long-term solutions to the structural problems the French economy was facing. In 2024, he called snap elections to blunt the far-right momentum. After the elections, he invited a leader from smaller blocs to form a government to keep the left-wing New Popular Front, the largest bloc, out of power, deepening the political crisis and weakening his position. This is Emmanuel Macron’s legacy. Worse, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right, anti-immigrant National Rally, could exploit the chaos and public anger to her benefit ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

item.title: Unknown vulnerabilities: on the cybersecurity advisory by CERT-In
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: India must strengthen its systems to detect and prevent data breaches
item.content:encoded:
India must strengthen its systems to detect and prevent data breaches

The cybersecurity advisory by the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has outlined two threat vectors vis-à-vis Indian commercial and government IT infrastructure: AI companies testing autonomous agents exceeding their designated operational constraints and bad actors weaponising open-source agentic AI tools for automated reconnaissance and exploitation. However, the organisations affected by recent breaches that the advisory was based on did not detect them: they came to light in the AI companies’ disclosures and CERT-In operations. Aside from developers allowing experimental systems to act outside their authorised bounds, the advisory highlights two problems for India — existing arrangements focus on cybersecurity incidents after they are revealed; and the implicated organisations being found under-prepared for the DPDP Act — to be enforced from 2027, including steep penalties on entities not maintaining reasonable safeguards against breaches. While CERT-In observed or received reports of 29.4 lakh incidents in 2025, it does not routinely publish postmortem analyses and is exempt from the RTI Act. As a result, public accountability is also weak: CERT-In found that the AI agents and/or bad actors exploited vulnerabilities, including exposed passwords, that are known security problems separate from AI agents’ abilities.

AI companies and labs have made several disclosures this year of agents unexpectedly breaching real-world infrastructure worldwide during testing. For India, however, the legal boundaries specified by the IT Act 2000 leave open an accountability gap for autonomous agents without the backing of human intentions. A more specific lacuna is that while CERT-In requires an organisation to report an intrusion within six hours, many organisations remain incapable of, or unwilling to, discover it. The reporting deadline itself has not ensured detection. Overall, the national cybersecurity landscape is fragmented across a pastiche of enforceable requirements in some domains, advisory technical standards in others, and narrow AI-specific accountability in yet others. As human and autonomous threat actors become more sophisticated, India needs to leapfrog to a landscape with enforceable risk-based requirements for both testing and defending against autonomous agents; better spotting unauthorised access, especially in the public sector; and a legal safe-harbour for security research conducted in good faith, in line with CERT-In policy. CERT-In should also publish more information, anonymised where necessary, which includes remediation outcomes and whether the affected individuals were informed. Finally, the government should also review the exemption for CERT-In from the RTI Act as such a sweeping exemption is unnecessary for effective cyber-defence.

item.title: Beyond religiosity: on the Kolkata pandal tragedy

item.description: Better crowd management and safety measures could have prevented the Kolkata pandal tragedy
item.content:encoded:
Better crowd management and safety measures could have prevented the Kolkata pandal tragedy

This year’s Durga Puja in Kolkata was meant to be truly special. The first after the Bharatiya Janata Party formed the government in West Bengal, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari wanted the pandals to showcase his party’s commitment to Hindu religiosity as well as to demonstrate the efficiency of the administrative machinery under him. He made it a point to highlight that the number of pandals in the State had increased by 25% over last year to more than 57,000. He was a visible presence at pandals across the city. Union Home Minister Amit Shah was in Kolkata as well to add heft and leverage to the puja’s popular appeal. But disaster struck at Kolkata’s Girish Park area on Saturday, as 19 people lost their lives in a stampede that could have been avoided with better organisation and crowd regulation. Both the police and the puja organisers failed to anticipate the sudden surge of the crowd at the venue.

Puja pandals, just like Mumbai’s Ganapati installations, are often sites of creativity and festivity; they have generally been accident-free despite the participation of a large number of people. The Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durgotstab’s theme this year was Beyond Sound. With a narrow entry and exit, the creators apparently sought to give an experience to visitors that involved controlling the light falling inside. The surrounding lanes were narrow city gullies that cannot hold two cars at the same time. Unanticipated too — at a time of retreat of the monsoon — was the rain that struck India’s east coast with heavy thunder and lightning in the evening. As people barged into the pandal seeking safety — visitors keep moving inside the Durga Puja pandals typically — the organisers requested people to leave fearing that the structure might collapse. Packed crowds can be incident-free only if sudden surges of movement, often triggered by panic, are avoided throughout. In Kolkata, panic apparently stemmed from the announcement regarding the safety of the structure, though the fear about the structure’s safety was justified. The effort should have been to wean the crowd away in a regulated manner. The government has promised an inquiry and deterrent follow-up action. There is the question of whether in the government’s drive to make the celebrations spectacular and grand, safe management practices got ignored at the event. Although Mr. Adhikari said the police helped rush the victims to hospitals, he also indicated that only temporary home guards had been posted at the pandal. Effective deployment of experienced police personnel may have helped avoid the tragedy.

item.title: Treacherous waters: on the Bihar boat tragedy
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: River crossings on stretches of the Ganga in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are notoriously unsafe
item.content:encoded:
River crossings on stretches of the Ganga in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are notoriously unsafe

River crossings on stretches of the Ganga in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are notoriously unsafe as poorly lit, unregistered boats ply with bare access to lifesaving equipment. Overcrowded vessels, operated by untrained or underaged people, add to the risks, and enforcement action only follows an accident. These boats are not the preserve of the poor but are also used by government personnel, teachers, and bank employees: many areas lack reliable alternatives, making the riverine journeys the sole option. On October 13, at least 13 children drowned when a country-made boat capsized in Raghopur, in Bihar’s Vaishali district, after setting off at 8.30 p.m. for a memorial feast in an adjoining village, even though rides are prohibited post sunset. The boat was visibly dilapidated, including a hole in the deck through which it drew water, and was being operated by a young boatman. There were at least half a dozen other people on the vessel when it capsized despite its reported capacity having been five. The riverine tract in Raghopur is continuously shaped by sediment deposits and has historically been hard to access, especially during the monsoons. Raghopur lacks all-weather roads, and has a history of being isolated during floods. The first section of the Kachchi Dargah-Bidupur bridge, between Patna and Raghopur, was ready in June 2025, but the monsoons still flooded the approach road and blocked access. The overarching motif across these episodes has been a consistent lack of safer alternatives, including the general paucity of public transport. A chaotic regulatory framework, including the Model Rules 2011 under the Bengal Ferries Act 1885 and the Inland Vessels Act 2021, has also not prevented training programmes and inspections from lagging behind the proliferation of unsafe transport practices.

That all those who drowned on October 13 were children deepens the sense of tragedy. In general, children warrant additional, more sensitive socio-economic support. The Bombay High Court had recently upbraided the Maharashtra government for failing to arrange transportation for over 200 children from villages near Chandoli National Park and Sahyadri Tiger Reserve; they had to walk several kilometres to reach school, braving the risk of wildlife encounters. Such precarity persists in Hingoli, Palghar, and Nashik in Maharashtra alone; similar situations have also been created by school reorganisation programmes that do not sufficiently account for children’s safety when shuttering infeasible facilities. The children who drowned in Vaishali were not headed to school, but the risk exposure is paramount. The ultimate tragedy is that access to ordinary childhood activities remains contingent, in so many economically disadvantaged communities, on accepting dangers that public institutions already know how to prevent.

item.title: Privacy and transparency: On the RTI Act amendment, petitions
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act has delivered a body blow to the Right to Information Act by diluting one of the RTI's foundational sections
item.content:encoded:
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act has delivered a body blow to the Right to Information Act by diluting one of the RTI's foundational sections

On Monday, the Supreme Court of India referred a series of petitions challenging the amendment to Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information (RTI) Act by Section 44(3) of the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, to a Constitution Bench, recognising its “constitutional sensitivity”. The Chief Justice of India even remarked that the Court might “have to lay down what is meant by ‘personal information’”. The RTI Act, 2005 was enacted to create an informed citizenry and ensure state accountability, which is vital for a democracy. Over two decades later, the DPDP Act has delivered a body blow by diluting one of its foundational sections. Section 8(1)(j) originally allowed the withholding of personal information only if it had no relationship to any public activity or interest, or if its disclosure resulted in an unwarranted invasion of privacy. Crucially, the section included a “public interest override” as an integral feature of the 2005 Act, permitting disclosure if a Public Information Officer was satisfied that the larger public interest justified it. The DPDP amendment removes this override and prohibits the disclosure of “any information which relates to personal information”, amounting to a blanket ban. This enables rejecting requests concerning officials, procurement records, audit reports or public spending. In its campaign for the RTI, the Internet Freedom Foundation has highlighted a “legitimate uses” paradox here: while Section 7 of the DPDP Act allows the state to process personal data without consent, the RTI amendment prevents citizens from using similar principles to seek transparency from the state. Thus, while the government can monitor the citizen, the citizen is denied the ability to scrutinise the government.

This amendment also creates a severe “chilling effect” on the press. As argued in one of the writ petitions by The Reporters’ Collective, journalists could be classified as “data fiduciaries” under the DPDP Act and its Rules when collecting information for investigative reports. Non-compliance with the Act can attract fines up to ₹250 crore. Such a legal framework threatens reducing journalism to just publishing government releases. It is ironic that the DPDP Act provides exemptions to startups but omits similar protections for journalism. This is in sharp contrast with the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which balances privacy and transparency to ensure accountability. The Constitution Bench must refer to the judgment, Central Public Information Officer (2019), which held that personal information should remain private unless disclosure is necessary for the larger public interest. It is known that the RTI has significantly reduced state-citizen (this includes the poor) information asymmetry over two decades. Ensuring its survival is essential for a responsive government.

item.content:encoded:
The Election Commission of India’s announcement of a special summary revision of electoral rolls in 17 States and Union Territories can be seen as a corrective to the missteps in the SIR

The Election Commission of India (ECI)’s announcement of a special summary revision of electoral rolls in 14 States and three Union Territories is, on the face of it, a routine exercise. This annual exercise to enrol new electors was stalled last year due to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, and resumes with January 1, 2027 as the qualifying date. Seen alongside what is simultaneously going on, however, the exercise is a corrective to the missteps in the SIR. The ECI is also conducting a “special drive” to re-enrol those “left out”, using the original Form 6 without the ancestry declaration. It has capped Form 7 objections amid reports of bulk filings in several States and will release searchable electoral rolls in text PDFs to parties and candidates. Together, these measures add up to an implicit admission about the severe flaws in the SIR. The drive is the most telling. By dispensing with mapping to older rolls and logical-discrepancy checks, it concedes that the SIR’s insistence on them was unnecessary. For States that are going to polls early next year — Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Uttarakhand – this is a welcome opportunity to repair the truncated rolls prepared by the SIR. Those wrongly deleted can now be re-enrolled, and newly eligible electors can be added, without recourse to “logical discrepancy” checks or quasi-citizenship tests. The ECI must report re-enrolments (after deletion) separately from fresh enrolments and the special drive’s house-to-house visits must ensure that the burden of re-enrolment does not fall on the electors again.

For States that have already voted on the basis of SIR rolls, however, a number of questions remain. In West Bengal, appellate tribunals have disposed of barely 3% of the 38 lakh appeals, 22 lakh of them by deleted electors, and restored the electors in 93% of the cases decided. The ECI has yet to say whether these appellants can also use the new drive or what becomes of the tribunals. In States such as Bihar, where the gender ratio fell from 907 in the 2024 Lok Sabha rolls to 892 in the SIR rolls, young married women who were struck off must be allowed the opportunity to re-enrol. The Supreme Court of India, which upheld the SIR in May and is now hearing petitions concerning West Bengal, Delhi and the Commission’s conduct, should ensure that genuine voters are reinstated on the electoral rolls. The ECI’s 2002-03 guidelines show that a revision need not shift the burden on to the elector. Any future intensive revision must revert to that model. The corrective steps owe much to the sustained protests against the SIR. But they are not enough for accountability. The two Election Commissioners objected on record to decisions taken by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) of India, and their questions remain unanswered. The appointment process laid down in Anoop Baranwal, which the government got overturned in Parliament in 2023 and on which a two-judge Bench delivered a split verdict last month, must also be settled. And the official who presided over the flawed process, CEC Gyanesh Kumar, must resign.

item.title: Ripples from the future: On the Nobel Prize for Economics 2026
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics has been awarded for work that is particularly crucial in the current global context
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics has been awarded for work that is particularly crucial in the current global context

This year’s Nobel Prize in Economics has been awarded for work that is particularly crucial in the current global context. Implications from the work also have lessons for Indian policymakers, some of which have already been learnt, while others remain a work in progress. The crux of the research done by the laureates Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford is in quantifying the future-looking aspect of the consumption and pricing decisions made by households and companies, respectively. Bringing empirical backing and rigour to this aspect, as the laureates have done, has helped policymakers identify economically distressed segments of the population, implement more effective policies during supply shocks, and communicate their policies better. Mr. Hall’s research in particular has helped governments identify the exact proportion of consuming households that are living hand-to-mouth. This is of vital fiscal importance for countries such as India. At the moment, India provides free food to more than 81 crore people, based on estimates that are between 13 to 15 years old. Using data — as Mr. Hall’s research allows — to identify those who truly need help will streamline the government’s subsidy expenditure at a time when fiscal room is tight.

Mr. Woodford’s work brought to light the importance of companies’ future expectations when setting current prices. The private sector Purchasing Managers’ Index serves as a measure of companies’ expectations for a month ahead, but there is a need for a government survey for longer time periods. Another key aspect brought out by the laureates’ work is the need to effectively communicate policy decisions to the public. Apart from rare instances, the government has been sorely lacking in this regard. This lack has been seen time and again, such as during its attempts to pass the Farm Laws, Labour Codes, and Citizenship (Amendment) Act, to name a few. Households and companies feel more secure making economic decisions when there is medium term policy clarity and certainty. The framework developed by the Nobel laureates thus also highlights the sheer damage the war in West Asia is inflicting over and above the loss of life and asset damage. The future looks grim and uncertain, and its effects are rippling backwards in time to the present.

item.title: Good, not good enough: On India and the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: India has faced a harsh reality check at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games
item.content:encoded:
India has faced a harsh reality check at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games

Aspiring to host the Olympic Games in 2036, India faced a harsh reality check at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. Compared with the previous Hangzhou Games, where it won 106 medals with a 650-plus contingent, the country won 85 medals from around 500 athletes. The aggregate fell short of an internally projected figure of around 100 medals. It is likely to invite a thorough postmortem, given the hundreds of crores of public money spent on the athletes’ preparation. India laboured to 21 gold medals, seven fewer than in Hangzhou, after a late surge of 11 top honours in the last two days, driven by the exploits of archers, boxers, wrestlers, and hockey and cricket players. It tied with Uzbekistan but managed to retain its fourth spot on the strength of a bigger haul of silver. Thirteen of the gold medals came from team events, with cricket, kabaddi and hockey making a clean sweep of titles. It underscored a stark reality: the country needs to raise its bar in medal-fetching individual sports, such as athletics, swimming, gymnastics, fencing and cycling, which determine success in multi-disciplinary Games. China, the runaway winner with a massive aggregate of 341 medals, including 169 gold, secured 54 medals in swimming alone. Barring athletics, India stood nowhere.

On a brighter note, India fielded 310 debutants and recorded a marginal increase in its athlete-to-medal ratio ahead of Los Angeles 2028. Several historic performances provided reasons to rejoice. Seventeen-year-old rookie recurve archer Kumkum Mohod dismantling the Korean women’s hegemony to help the archery team contribute five gold medals was a defining moment. Trap shooter Neeru Dhanda, golfer Pranavi Urs, wrestler Sujeet Kalkal and the women’s hockey team, which upset Paris Olympics silver medallist China to clinch gold after 44 years, hogged the limelight. Lovlina Borgohain, Aman Sehrawat, Mirabai Chanu, Vithya Ramraj and Gulveer Singh lived up to their billing. Boxers, wrestlers and golfers registered noticeable improvement. Olympic quota places in archery and hockey added to the excitement. Indian women catching up with men — both genders delivered 38 medals apiece — was another encouraging sign. On the flip side, India’s two major contributors, athletics and shooting, which earned 24 and 15 medals, respectively, yielded 12 fewer medals than in 2023. The shuttlers slipped, while the tennis players returned empty-handed after 40 years. P.V. Sindhu and Manu Bhaker flopped. Stricter scrutiny of athletes’ funding and efficient implementation of the revamped Khelo India scheme, designed with a long-term vision, are essential for course correction. Without propelling India’s sporting standards, a bid to host the Olympics may become a countdown to international embarrassment.

item.title: Double standards: On the Trump diesel deal with Russia
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: The Trump diesel deal with Russia highlighrs the hypocrisy and strategic folly of the U.S.'s decisions, and is a lesson for countries which have been criticised and penalised for trading with Russia
item.content:encoded:
The Trump diesel deal with Russia highlighrs the hypocrisy and strategic folly of the U.S.'s decisions, and is a lesson for countries which have been criticised and penalised for trading with Russia

Last year, U.S. President Donald Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on India over India’s oil purchases from Russia. Peter Navarro, Mr. Trump’s trade czar, even called Russia’s invasion of Ukraine “Modi’s war”, saying India was funding the Russian aggression through energy deals. Last month, Mr. Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law, giving him the power to impose up to 100% tariffs on countries buying Russian energy, including India and China. And then, last week, Mr. Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel — releasing 300,000 tonnes immediately to the “American and global marketplace”, followed by 5,00,000 tonnes in November. Immediately after the announcement, the Treasury Department suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 7, 2027. Mr. Trump’s flip-flop is a lesson for countries such as India, which have been criticised and penalised for trading with Russia. The latest policy switch also exposes the incoherence in western strategic thinking. The West imposed sanctions on Russia’s energy sector to weaken Vladimir Putin’s “war machine”. Four years later, the U.S. began bombing Iran. When the Iran war drove up fuel prices, Washington temporarily eased sanctions on Russian fuel before striking a deal with Moscow.

Beyond the hypocrisy and strategic folly of the U.S. decisions, Mr. Trump’s diesel deal also marks the ineffectiveness of the western sanctions regime. When Russia attacked Ukraine in 2022, the West adopted a two-pronged response: weaken the Russian economy through sanctions and weaken the Russian military in Ukraine by arming Kyiv. The sanctions were a double-edged sword, hurting the Russian economy, but the curtailment of trade between Russia and Europe has also plunged European economies, particularly Germany, into deep crises. To offset the impact of the sanctions, Moscow looked east where China and India were willing to buy discounted Russian fuel. The episode also underscores the changes in the economic landscape. Mr. Trump’s U-turn leaves Ukraine and Europe in a spot, at a time when Moscow is escalating its bombardment of Ukraine and testing NATO’s resolve through grey-zone tactics. If Brussels thinks that prolonging the war would serve its strategic goal of bleeding Russia dry in Ukraine, it may be making a mistake, as Mr. Trump seems less interested in NATO’s collective defence or in the defence of Kyiv. Instead, their focus must shift to finding a diplomatic way out. If Mr. Trump can reach a diesel deal with Mr. Putin amid the war, he should work with the warring parties, his allies in Europe and his new partner in Moscow, to secure a ceasefire and ease Russia-NATO tensions. In the meantime, the U.S. and Europe could stop moralising to the Global South for doing trade with Russia.

item.title: Out of site: On Jantar Mantar denotification, protests and democracy
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: People’s protests are meant to be seen and heard, not pushed away from Jantar Mantar to the margins of the city of Delhi and hidden from the public eye
item.content:encoded:
People’s protests are meant to be seen and heard, not pushed away from Jantar Mantar to the margins of the city of Delhi and hidden from the public eye

The Delhi Police’s decision to denotify Jantar Mantar in the national capital as a site where protests can be organised has itself triggered a storm of protest over its sheer arbitrariness. The Delhi Police, which is under the Union Home Ministry, have told the Delhi High Court that Jantar Mantar was denotified as a protest site following a Supreme Court directive issued on October 9. The Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant had urged the Union government to identify an alternative protest site that is spacious and open. The order was passed while hearing petitions challenging the government’s decision to restrict movement within and into the city to halt the October 10 protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Observations were also exchanged that protests in and around Jantar Mantar were a source of inconvenience for ordinary commuters. It is possible to argue that protesters cause traffic congestion and inconvenience. But those arguments are valid only as much as similar arguments that are usually raised against democracy itself. There is a reactionary view that democracy delays decision-making, elections disrupt development and economic activity, and that there should therefore be fewer elections and less politics. The BJP’s push for simultaneous elections to Parliament and State Assemblies once every five years is based on the same logic, that at its heart questions the legitimacy of democracy itself. The argument against protests at Jantar Mantar does not hold water. It is antithetical to the concept of public deliberation and protest, which are central to democracy.

A centrally located site of protest is part of the urban space in most democracies, as in Washington DC and London. Public protesters are usually marginal groups who lack representation at the decision-making table. Street protest is actually an outcome of their lack of power, and an instrument for people with no other way of being heard. To keep them far away from the seat of power and render them invisible is a violent police argument against their very attempt to be heard and seen. The reason why a protester wants to be in Jantar Mantar is its proximity to the centre of power — it is located close to the Parliament complex, and the President’s Estate. If, in the name of public order, they are pushed far away into the margins of the city, as is now being sought, it is equivalent to keeping them trapped in the very situation they are trying to escape. If protests can happen only far away from the seat of power, the logic can easily be extended to argue that people must stay at home and protest. That is not how a democracy works.

item.title: Spiralling food prices: on rising inflation
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: September’s retail inflation marks the fourth consecutive month that price increases have kept headline CPI above the RBI's 4% target with the impact particularly severe for rural India
item.content:encoded:
September’s retail inflation marks the fourth consecutive month that price increases have kept headline CPI above the RBI's 4% target with the impact particularly severe for rural India

September’s retail inflation, at 5.54%, an almost two-year high, marks the fourth consecutive month that price increases have kept headline CPI above the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) 4% target. The impact has been particularly severe for rural Indians, whose inflation rate reached 6.08%. Rural food inflation rose almost two percentage points between August and September, touching 8.06%. Onion (108.09%), garlic (54.62%) and ginger (62.85%) drove the surge, even as potato (-11.50%) and tomato (-8.62%) prices remained below year-earlier levels. The festive season ahead will be expensive for rural households already facing the uncertainties of a deficient monsoon, El Niño-related risks to harvests and incomes, and unusually high temperatures. Headline CPI is now just 0.46 percentage points below the RBI’s upper tolerance limit of 6%. The Monetary Policy Committee raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% in October, ending a pause that began after its previous increase in February 2023. Another increase in December cannot be ruled out if price pressures continue to broaden. Chief among the factors driving inflation since the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran have been fuel, food and transport, compounded by a depreciating rupee.

The Indian crude basket, according to the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell, rose from $82.04 a barrel in July to $116.09 in September — a 41% increase — with economy-wide implications for freight, production and distribution. The RBI’s special dollar facility for oil marketing companies may ease spot-market pressure on the rupee, but only temporarily if the underlying import dependence and geopolitical risks persist. The crucial subgroup, transport services for goods, recorded inflation of 14.73% in September, up from 14.64% in August. Restaurant and accommodation services inflation has reached 9.36%, while inflation in personal care, social protection and miscellaneous goods and services, which include precious metals, has moderated to 13.75%. Core inflation, excluding food and fuel but including precious metals, rose to 4.6% in September from 4.16% in August, suggesting that price pressures are broadening. Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have pulled a record ₹3.08 trillion ($32.73 billion) out of Indian equities in the nine months ending September this year, which is almost double that of the whole of CY2025. FPIs have been net sellers in six of the past nine months as they seek safe havens, stronger dollar-denominated returns, and bond yields. Selling resumed in October, adding to pressure on the rupee, which weakened by about 7% against the dollar over the year to early October, despite RBI interventions such as direct dollar sales and attracting foreign-currency inflows. The central bank’s latest steps have helped the rupee recover, but cannot resolve the underlying pressures. With crude prices elevated, the rupee vulnerable and no clear end to the West Asia conflict, imported inflation is likely to continue shaping domestic prices in the months ahead.

item.title: Illogical reasons: On The Hindu’s investigation of Delhi’s draft rolls
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: The Hindu’s investigation of Delhi’s draft rolls and the names that the ECI flagged as 'logical discrepancies' shows that the process is not only exclusionary but also insidious
item.content:encoded:
The Hindu’s investigation of Delhi’s draft rolls and the names that the ECI flagged as 'logical discrepancies' shows that the process is not only exclusionary but also insidious

That the ECI’s SIR of electoral rolls has been flawed by design and tuned to exclude genuine electors rather than ensure their full enrolment is now well established. The Hindu’s investigation of Delhi’s draft rolls and the names that the ECI flagged as “logical discrepancies” shows that the process is not only exclusionary but also insidious. The arbitrary nature of these “discrepancies”, especially those relating to family size, suggests that they were chosen to target communities with higher, though declining, fertility rates, for exclusion. Muslims make up 13.6% of Delhi’s draft rolls — in line with the 2011 Census — but accounted for 20.3% of those flagged for “logical discrepancies”. This number goes up to 30% for those flagged under the five reasons linked to family size. None of these criteria bears on the eligibility of an elector, who should be an Indian citizen, at least 18, ordinarily resident in the constituency and should not be disqualified under the law. Following Lal Babu Hussein (1995), a name on an earlier electoral roll has probative value as evidence of citizenship and cannot be struck off without inquiry. The children an elector has, a parent’s age at the elector’s birth or name spelling are unconnected; neither the ECI’s Manual on Electoral Rolls (2023) nor its SIR of 2002-03 provided for such checks.

When the ECI began the SIR in Bihar, the enrolment and claims and objections phases had their infirmities but there was no direct or indirect discrimination by religion. The Hindu estimated that 18.4% of those deleted from Bihar’s pre-SIR rolls were Muslims, in line with their population share (17.7%, 2011 Census). But in the SIR’s Phase 2 in West Bengal, the ECI introduced the “logical discrepancies” check midway. Electors already on draft rolls were flagged on unexplained criteria with ECINET software rather than the statutory Electoral Registration Officers deciding on who got flagged. The impact was severe — 27 lakh electors were deleted following adjudication by judicial officers, after being flagged overwhelmingly for “logical discrepancies”; 22 lakh appealed but just 1,607 electors were reinstated in time for the vote. By September, nearly 93% of the 1.26 lakh appeals that were decided had restored electors to the rolls — an indication of large-scale disenfranchisement before the vote. A sample-based analysis of those excluded after adjudication estimated a much higher share of Muslims than their population share. The same process has now been carried over to Phase 3, including Delhi, where The Hindu’s investigation shows a clear skew against Muslim electors. The Supreme Court must now halt the SIR, as a process built on arbitrary criteria with no basis in electoral law, and which discriminates against specific communities, should not be allowed to firm up electoral rolls.

Punjab grapples with drug trafficking and targeted killings

A chemist has been charged with killing anti-drug-trafficking activist Parvinder Singh Jhota after his allegedly illegal drug business came under threat. Separately, social media influencer Mad Sandhu was allegedly the victim of a premeditated, transnational syndicate hit that used inter-State escape routes. Both events in Punjab involved digital platforms and both events expose a dire gap in public safety. While Mr. Jhota’s alleged murderer was a local chemist, the macro-level drug trade in Punjab is intertwined with gangster networks, with the cross-border drug smuggling known to be a key source of illicit funds. Together with a string of targeted killings of police personnel and local politicians, the incidents depict a Punjab caught between local drug trafficking and citizens resorting to vigilantism and crime syndicates carrying out assassinations with disquieting ease. Some events have also raised suspicions of cross-border support and a demand to involve enforcement agencies. The AIIMS Magnitude of Substance Use in India survey estimated that in 2017-18 — the latest year for which it is available — 1.28% of Punjab’s population aged 10-75 years had an opioid dependence, versus 0.26% nationally. NCRB data also recorded 106 drug overdose deaths in 2024 versus 89 in 2023, in Punjab, likely an undercount since attribution depends on medical certification and excludes long-term complications and unhygienic habits associated with drug use.

Punjab’s geopolitical location renders it an important entry point and market, with the security apparatus hampered by smugglers using multiple transport modes. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime reported in June that India’s pharmaceutical and chemicals industries also provide bad actors with ample opportunities to divert controlled substances or precursors for illicit use. The State’s ‘Yugh Nashian Virudh’ campaign of 2025 has also claimed 68,850 arrests of alleged traffickers and the attachment or confiscation of assets valued ₹319 crore. However, cases registered differ from convictions and asset attachment differs from forfeiture. Mr. Jhota’s hostile tactics also enjoyed public support, and authorities need to examine why the people are overlooking formal reporting channels. Under its narcotics policy, the State has to reduce the availability of harmful drugs, disrupt wholesale supply chains, identify corrupt facilitators, and expand access to rehabilitative care. Paralleling investigations into the coordination of targeted killings, an anti-trafficking strategy must also probe the financing and logistics of networks, to dismantle institutional collusion, and better protect threatened individuals.

item.title: The sound and the fiery: on green crackers, pollution control
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: Green crackers offer little relief from air and noise pollution
item.content:encoded:
Green crackers offer little relief from air and noise pollution

As Delhi and the National Capital Region (NCR) head into another winter, they must brace for the return of a foe kept on a leash that is alternately loosened or tightened. In November 2016, the Supreme Court of India suspended licences for the sale of fireworks in the NCR after Deepavali celebrations pushed PM2.5 levels above 700 g/m³. The Court relaxed the suspension in September 2017, partly to protect existing licence holders and livelihoods, but restored the suspension for Deepavali in October. In 2018, in its judgment in Arjun Gopal and Others vs Union of India and Others, the Court allowed only reduced-emission and “green” crackers, banned joined firecrackers or laris, and imposed a two-hour window. The latest order permits specified next-generation joined green crackers, while declining a total ban on fireworks, invoking public sentiment. Fire crackers are far from the smoking gun of Delhi’s air-quality crisis. Construction dust, vehicles, stubble burning and stagnant, cold air all contribute to winter pollution. But when these push the air towards “severe” levels, crackers can produce an acute spike. In 2025, the first Deepavali after the Court permitted limited use of green crackers, Delhi’s post-Deepavali PM2.5 average reached 488 g/m³, the highest since 2021, while hourly concentrations peaked at 675 g/m³.

There is no gainsaying that green crackers are a pyrrhic green. The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research–National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-NEERI), which promoted them, says the newer generation promises a 45%-60% cut in PM10. These figures, however, do not reflect real-world conditions, and when “cleaner” crackers are burst in greater numbers, the savings in particulate pollution evaporate. This is without accounting for noise pollution. There is also the difficulty of enforcement. The Commission for Air Quality Management has stated that QR codes had been sold to unregistered manufacturers — registered manufacturers reportedly sold them, allowing unauthorised firecrackers to be passed off as certified green crackers. The explosives regulator had no testing facility in Delhi. In 2018 and 2019, the police could not distinguish green crackers from conventional ones. Unless fireworks manufacturing moves into the formal sector, regulations are followed in practice, and awareness of the toll on public health spreads among those who love the sound and fury of crackers, air and noise pollution are here to stay.

item.title: Drought report: On southwest monsoon, drought in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: In drought management after the retreat of the southwest monsoon, the Centre must release support as soon as the findings of the Inter-Ministerial Central Team have been publicly verified
item.content:encoded:
In drought management after the retreat of the southwest monsoon, the Centre must release support as soon as the findings of the Inter-Ministerial Central Team have been publicly verified

A substantial drought seems to be inflicting Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh after the crucial southwest monsoon concluded with a significant deficiency in the most-affected regions. The national drought framework combines agricultural and hydrological indicators and ground-truthing studies, including before a distressed State can access additional support from the NDRF. In June-September, Karnataka reportedly suffered a close to 35% rainfall deficit. The government has since declared 217 of 240 taluks to be drought-hit with extensive damage to red gram, maize, cotton, and sugarcane cultivation. Andhra Pradesh experienced a shortfall of 53% in June-August and 388 of 688 mandals have been declared drought-hit. Horticulture crops over nearly 18,000 hectares are now at risk. Karnataka has also petitioned the Centre for ₹11,000 crore from the NDRF along with higher input subsidies. Andhra Pradesh has set aside ₹190 crore to protect horticultural crops and has directed drinking water conservation. The summer monsoon had its poorest showing since 2015 this year. There have been warnings of the effects of the strengthening El Niño, although an attribution study elucidating the strength of causal relationships in the present instance is pending.

In a previous era, drought declarations were beset by subjective claims, sometimes exaggerated to maximise state support. Since 2009, however, the Manual for Drought Management and updates to it and Finance Commission decisions have tightened the process. While States still have some incentives to expand their declarations, the Centre has also resisted releasing NDRF assistance before, including with Karnataka in 2024, while also increasing their own relief obligations. The Centre must desist from frustrating States and release support as soon as the findings of the Inter-Ministerial Central Team have been publicly verified. In addition to mitigating indebtedness among farmers and expanding access to relief beyond land ownership, the States also need more discipline vis-à-vis storing water and rationalising consumption. Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka have offered incentives and advisories, including to adopt micro-irrigation and to cultivate less water-intensive crops, but have not imposed binding limits. The Centre may also consider incentives to resist drought, even in the face of a deficient monsoon, because the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has been warning of expanding drought-like conditions in South Asia, and broadening agricultural insurance. It must certainly not use the prospect of the more protracted, more imprudent river-interlinking project as an excuse to overlook pro-resilience aims such as sustainably using groundwater and choosing crops based on local rainfall and aquifers and availability of income support.

item.content:encoded:
Ruling parties sweep the bypolls in Nandigram, Rejinagar, Thattanchavady, Dharapuram and Madurantakam but defections cloud the Tamil Nadu results

The by-election results in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, declared on Friday, held few surprises. Barely five months after the April Assembly elections, the ruling party in each State/UT won all five bypolls. What varied was the scale of victory. In West Bengal, the BJP retained Nandigram and wrested Rejinagar, with strong vote shares of 76% and 63%. In Puducherry, the ruling All India N.R. Congress also registered an emphatic win — 61% of the votes — in Thattanchavady. Nandigram and Thattanchavady were vacated by the Chief Ministers, which partly explains the strong wins. But the contests in Tamil Nadu were closer. Dharapuram and Madurantakam fell vacant after their AIADMK MLAs resigned and defected to the ruling TVK, which renominated them. Both won their seats back with 37% and 40% of the vote, respectively, leading the DMK rival candidates by about eight percentage points. By-elections tend to favour the party in power, as voters prefer representatives with access to government. But the variance between West Bengal and Tamil Nadu reflects the nature of contest in two similarly sized States but with vastly different political cultures.

In West Bengal, Assembly victories have for decades worked as a winner-take-all mandate, which the ruling party extends to panchayat and by-elections. The pattern took shape during the Left Front’s long rule, became entrenched during the Trinamool Congress’s 15 years in power and is visible in the BJP’s tenure so far. In these contests, Opposition parties have performed far worse than in Assembly and Lok Sabha elections. In Tamil Nadu, however, a three-way contest now has kept politics competitive. The wins have helped the TVK improve its tally to 109 in the House with a sanctioned membership of 234, but the narrow margins, despite a no-holds-barred campaign by Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, suggest that the expected honeymoon effect did not fully materialise. The DMK, now the TVK’s principal rival, has shown that it still has a solid base despite its abrupt defeat in May. For the AIADMK, finishing third in the seats it won in May only deepens worries about its decline. Its leadership will now face sharper questions about whether it can hold on to its legislators. Four more AIADMK MLAs had joined the TVK and their seats will go to bypolls. This is a regressive turn in Tamil Nadu. MLAs are resigning barely months, sometimes days, into their terms to share in the loaves and fishes of office and the ruling party re-fields them. This defeats the spirit of the anti-defection law and overrides the Assembly election mandate. That the electorate rewarded these manoeuvres should worry anyone who is concerned about the quality of representation.

item.content:encoded:
By awarding the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navi Pillay, the Nobel committee has sought not only to restore its credibility but also to strengthen voices defending international law

By awarding the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navi Pillay, the Norwegian Nobel committee has sought not only to restore its credibility, tarnished by controversial decisions in the recent past, but also to strengthen the voices defending international law. Ms. Pillay served on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court (ICC), and chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Born in Durban in 1941 to a family of Indian Tamil origin, Ms. Pillay grew up in apartheid South Africa, opened her own legal firm in the 1960s and defended anti-apartheid political prisoners and activists on the notorious Robben Island, including Nelson Mandela. Her contributions as a jurist have shaped international criminal law. In 1998, as a part of the Rwanda war crimes tribunal, she co-authored the judgment against Jean-Paul Akayesu, a local politician, recognising that rape and sexual violence constitute acts of genocide. Last year, the Palestine commission that she led concluded that Israel had committed acts of genocide in Gaza and that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide” in their speeches and statements. Compared to Barack Obama, the 2009 winner who bombed Libya two years later, or Maria Corina Machado, the 2025 winner who supported Washington’s economic strangulation of Venezuela and its illegal strikes on boats in the Caribbean, Ms. Pillay has an untarnished record of standing up for the victims of international crimes.

Ms. Pillay has been honoured at a time when the world is witnessing conflicts, which have effectively jeopardised the law-based international order. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is a challenge to the fundamental principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity. Israel continues to bomb Gaza, Syria and Lebanon and tighten its occupation of Palestinian territories, with impunity. The U.S. under President Donald Trump — who believes he deserved a Nobel Prize — started a war on Iran on February 28 and killed its Supreme Leader, a flagrant violation of international law and norms. He has also launched a frontal attack on international institutions, including the ICC that has been placed under sanctions. What prevents the world from becoming a Hobbesian jungle where the mighty do as they please is the existence of international law and institutions that hold them accountable. The message of the 2026 Peace Prize is that the fight to strengthen those rules and institutions is part of the struggle for a more peaceful and accountable world.

The right to organise, assemble, and speak is at the core of democracy, and the curtailment of any of the fundamental rights is a curtailment of democracy itself

The Constitution of India guarantees all citizens the fundamental right to peaceful assembly and protest. The right to organise, assemble, and speak is at the core of democracy, and the curtailment of any of the fundamental rights is a curtailment of democracy itself. That being the promise of the Constitution to every citizen, regardless of gender, caste, or status, it is unsettling that the Government of India under Prime Minister Narendra Modi is brazenly knocking down those rights through police high-handedness across the country, particularly in Delhi, the capital. Youth and student organisations, such as the CJP, the AISA, SFI and AISF, had called for a peaceful protest on October 10. Instead of ensuring peaceful assembly, as per the law of the land, the Centre ordered a countrywide swoop, where thousands of young people were taken into preventive detention and Delhi was locked down as if under martial law. Trains were cancelled and stopped, passengers waylaid, and journalists, activists, academics, and lawyers assaulted and detained, all in shocking misuse and weaponisation of the law against democracy itself. In the heart of Delhi, police personnel without identification badges have been recorded on video. What Delhi witnessed on Saturday was a repeat, in a greater degree, of the police high-handedness in July against youth protesters. Despite video evidence of male police personnel assaulting women protesters during that episode, months later, neither the government nor the Supreme Court of India has held anyone accountable for the law enforcement excesses.

On October 9, the Court had said that a blanket ban on travel or assembly could not be allowed. But that is exactly what was done in Delhi, as people, including several former Chief Ministers, senior politicians, and lawyers, were rounded up from around the city. On Sunday, the Court, in its hearing, acknowledged the urgency and seriousness of the issue, and repeated its directives. But piecemeal orders and half-hearted lamentations by the Court have had no restraining impact on a government that seems to be doubling down on its practice of branding critics as foreign agents and anti-nationals instead of coming clean on its record. The BJP government is going this far in defence of an official — the Chief Election Commissioner of India, Gyanesh Kumar. Instead of calling for accountability from the Election Commission of India, which has disenfranchised millions of Indians in a clear act of illegality, the BJP and its central and State governments are deploying the strong arm of the state to defend him. item.title: Delivery completed: On the GST Council meet, reforms
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: With the latest round of reforms, GST could finally live up to its promise of becoming a good and simple tax
item.content:encoded:
With the latest round of reforms, GST could finally live up to its promise of becoming a good and simple tax

The decisions taken by the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council in its 57th meeting on Thursday reveal two distinct changes in the attitude of the tax administration: increased trust in the taxpayer, and reduced anxiety over tax revenues. This is a big change from the system in place so far, where taxpayers have been bogged down by compliance requirements, and the tax enforcement has used this complexity to try to extract every rupee it can. The data show gross collections have not often deviated significantly from the mean over the last two years. After nine years, taxpayers have also become familiar, if not comfortable, with the tax filing system. The previous meeting also rectified most rate-related issues in GST and even reduced the number of slabs, a major driver of the complexity of the tax system. The time was ripe for a significant overhaul of the processes and administration of GST, and the Council has delivered. Thursday’s reforms address complications in the entire chain of GST paperwork, from registration and return filing, to refunds and litigation. The thrust is to reduce human discretion in these processes by automating registrations, reducing the number of times small businesses have to file returns, handling refunds through computer-based verification, and significantly reducing the powers of GST officers. In essence, trust the taxpayer to comply, and crack down only when non-compliance is demonstrable. That is the way it should be, instead of a ‘guilty until proven innocent’ approach.

While all the simplification measures are welcome, some specific ones deserve special mention as they will substantially ease areas of major discontent. So far, taxpayers were denied input tax credits (ITC) until their suppliers had filed their returns. This meant that thousands of genuine businesses that had received supplies and paid taxes on them were denied ITC, leading to a drying up of crucial working capital. The GST Council has tasked a committee to find a solution that can be implemented by April 1. Removing the arrest powers of GST officers is another step that will significantly reduce harassment, as will tightening the rules around inspection, searches, and seizures of consignments. The Centre has also used this opportunity to introduce a faceless assessment system for Central GST registered companies, along the lines of the popular faceless system in income tax. The decision to review rates only once a year, and implement rate changes only at the start of financial years, removes significant uncertainty that usually arises each time the Council meets. In its 10th year, GST is finally starting to look like what it should have at the time of rollout.

item.title: Beyond forms: On the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
item.dc:creator: The Hindu Editorial
item.description: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature awarded to Anne Carson celebrates her literary experimentation, imaginative daring and innovative use of language
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature awarded to Anne Carson celebrates her literary experimentation, imaginative daring and innovative use of language

Every year, before the announcement of the Nobel Prize in Literature, there is strong speculation among literary critics about the possible contenders. The Swedish Academy, which keeps its nominations secret for 50 years, has often sprung surprises. But this year, it has chosen a bookmaker’s favourite in Anne Carson, the 76-year-old Canadian poet, essayist, translator, and dramatist. It has also kept in tune with its decade-old trend of recognising women writers every two or three years — Carson is the 19th woman among the 123 Nobel laureates in literature. The Academy praised her “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”. Known for continually dismantling the boundaries between poetry, prose, and scholarship, Carson seamlessly brings the classical in conversation with the contemporary and personal, often through strange juxtapositions. She has also frequently collaborated with theatre directors, choreographers, and visual artists, expanding our understanding of what constitutes literature.

A scholar of classics and ancient Greek, Carson’s works explore love, desire, mysticism, antiquity, and despair. Her first book, Eros the Bittersweet (1986), a reworked version of her PhD thesis on Sappho, examines the pleasure and pain of desire through the Greek idea of lack. Short Talks (1992) is a series of brief, lyric prose poems, each approaching its subject through fragments and shifts in voice. In Autobiography of Red (1998), perhaps her best-known work, she reimagines the ancient Greek myth of Geryon and Heracles as a queer coming-of-age story, combining poetry and prose. The Beauty of the Husband (2001), a semi-autobiographical work of narrative verse about the painful disintegration of a marriage, borrows its imagery from tango while opening its sections with lines from John Keats; she became the first woman to win the T.S. Eliot Prize for it. Her later works — Nox (2010), which is at once a book, an elegy, and an art object; Red Doc (2013), a sequel to Autobiography of Red; and Float (2016), which takes the form of 22 chapbooks housed in an acetate case — all resist easy categorisation. The Prize is thus not just a recognition of an outstanding poet or classicist, but also a celebration of literary experimentation and a reminder of the limitless possibilities of human imagination and creativity at a time of AI slop. In an age of polarised debates, her writing never simplifies the complexities of human experience or forces them into neat conclusions. By reworking classical traditions in unexpected ways, she makes the ancient feel startlingly contemporary while retaining a sense of its historical specificity. The Academy has chosen a writer who belongs in no category in particular, and everywhere at once.
